The terms are $3\cdot\tfrac14,\; 3\cdot\tfrac1{16},\; 3\cdot\tfrac1{64}, \dots$, a geometric series with first term $a = \tfrac34$ (the value for $r = 1$) and common ratio $\rho = \tfrac14$.

Since $|\rho| = \tfrac14 < 1$ the series converges, and $S_\infty = \dfrac{a}{1 - \rho}$:
$$\sum_{r=1}^{\infty} 3\left(\frac14\right)^r = \frac{\tfrac34}{1 - \tfrac14} = \frac{\tfrac34}{\tfrac34} = 1.$$

$$\boxed{\sum_{r=1}^{\infty} 3\left(\tfrac14\right)^r = 1}$$

(Alternative: $3\sum_{r=1}^{\infty}\left(\tfrac14\right)^r = 3\cdot\dfrac{1/4}{1 - 1/4} = 3\cdot\tfrac13 = 1$.)

questions.enonce_markdown: The sum of the first $n$ terms of a series is given by $S_n = 2n^2 + n$. Find an expression for the $n^{th}$ term of the series. (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
The $n^{th}$ term is the difference of consecutive partial sums, $u_n = S_n - S_{n-1}$ for $n \ge 2$:
$$u_n = (2n^2 + n) - \left[2(n - 1)^2 + (n - 1)\right] = 2n^2 + n - (2n^2 - 4n + 2 + n - 1) = 4n - 1.$$

For $n = 1$: $u_1 = S_1 = 2 + 1 = 3$, and the formula gives $4(1) - 1 = 3$, so it holds for all $n \ge 1$.

$$\boxed{u_n = 4n - 1}$$

questions.enonce_markdown: The sum of the first $n$ terms of a series is given by $S_n = 2n^2 + n$. Show that the series is an arithmetic progression. (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
From part (a), $u_n = 4n - 1$ for every $n \ge 1$. For $n \ge 2$:
$$u_n - u_{n-1} = (4n - 1) - \left(4(n - 1) - 1\right) = 4,$$
a constant independent of $n$.

A sequence whose consecutive terms differ by a constant is an arithmetic progression. Here the first term is $a = u_1 = 3$ and the common difference is $d = 4$ (terms $3, 7, 11, 15, \dots$). $\blacksquare$

(Check with the sum formula $S_n = \dfrac n2\left[2a + (n - 1)d\right] = \dfrac n2(6 + 4n - 4) = n(2n + 1) = 2n^2 + n$.)
